body.text: Two years into his presidency, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto maintains the support of a large political coalition. The large size of his cabinet has allowed the president to include a wide range of figures, political parties, and civil society representatives in his camp. In his speech at Nahdlatul Ulama (NU)’s 35th Congress in August 2026, Prabowo cited the need for political stability in order to maintain his large political coalition.

Unlike his predecessors, Prabowo arguably enjoyed a relatively smooth transition period, given his pledge of continuity from his predecessor Joko “Jokowi.” Prabowo’s large “rainbow coalition” has helped him establish a seemingly stable political condition. However, as the current cabinet consists of 49 ministers and 57 vice ministers, some challenges remain, namely overlapping authority, over-centralization, and sluggish policy execution.

In addition, the next general election in 2029 could potentially test Prabowo’s large political coalition. The ongoing discussions on the revision of the Elections Law will certainly stimulate intra-coalition dynamics, notably amongst the government’s political party supporters. Maintaining coalition cohesion and the internal dynamics of his own Gerindra party will be another challenge for Prabowo.
Rainbow Coalitions and Political Stability

In 1999, Indonesia adopted a proportional representation (PR) system for its parliamentary elections. The system – and the electoral threshold for parliamentary and presidential elections first enacted in 2004 – means that very few Indonesian political parties (with occasional exceptions) can nominate a presidential candidate on their own due to the inability to meet the presidential threshold. It necessitates the need for a large coalition to make a presidential candidacy viable.

Hence, every Post-Reformasi Indonesian government has formed a “rainbow coalition” government consisting of almost every major party represented in the parliament, key interest groups like the Indonesian military (TNI), and civil society organizations like NU – Indonesia’s largest Islamic organization. This began under presidents Abdurrahman Wahid (1999 to 2001) and Megawati Sukarnoputri (2001 to 2004), each of whom formed a coalition government consisting of almost all parliamentary parties.

Subsequent presidential elections have continued this practice, usually with the winning presidential candidate possessing a charismatic persona that enables them to gain a large number of votes in the presidential elections, as former presidents Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono and Jokowi did. Nonetheless, the popularity and the ability to attract a plurality of votes did not always come in handy in terms of maintaining political stability after the general election was over. Yudhoyono and Jokowi learnt this harsh lesson in the early days of their presidencies. Their initially minority political coalition failed to provide the much-needed political support to pass legislation, let alone provide political stability.

A smaller political coalition means that the executive is likely to face resistance in pushing the agenda, especially policies requiring parliamentary approval. Jokowi even at one time had to go toe-to-toe with his former primary party supporter, the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle (PDIP).

Hence, beyond forming a pact with political parties, securing the support of the military and police became part of the plan to enhance presidential coalitions. Both Yudhoyono and Jokowi also included figures representing interest groups, such as businesses and religious organizations like NU and Muhammadiyah as cabinet members. Here, the pragmatic goal of achieving political stability plays a major role in building a political coalition.
The Limits of the Rainbow Coalition

Although a large coalition may deliver political stability, a big-tent, rainbow coalition approach has created new challenges of its own. First, friction between coalition members is likely. Each of the coalition’s constituent forces, whether a political party, a civil society organization, or a state institution, has its own interests. This can create a collision of claims and goals between the members of the coalition.

These tensions may be sharpened by the current government’s budget-efficiency drive, which has further concentrated control over state spending in the president’s hands. This means fewer state resources are available for coalition partners to channel to their clients and constituencies. As the 2029 election draws closer, competition among them for what remains is likely to intensify.

Second, holding such a broad coalition together requires constant tinkering to satisfy not only the demands of coalition members but also the agendas of their leaders. Frequent reshuffling of this kind puts the effectiveness of policy implementation under strain.

As of October 15, President Prabowo has conducted eight cabinet reshuffles. In addition, any change to key cabinet positions can unsettle the internal dynamics of the coalition members themselves, particularly the parties and mass organizations whose figures are moved in or out.

Third, expanding the cabinet to accommodate coalition partners has blurred the lines of authority. Political heavyweights with access to the president’s inner circle carry more influence than colleagues without access, regardless of the portfolios they hold. As a result, some ministries enjoy greater clout than others simply because of who leads them. These blurred lines of authority also slow down decision-making, a serious disadvantage when the government faces emergencies that require cross-sectoral coordination, such as the 2025 Sumatra floods, the 2026 Flores earthquake, and the ongoing forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan.
Towards the 2029 Elections

With the 2029 general election slowly approaching, maintaining the cohesion of his rainbow political coalition will be a challenge for Prabowo. As mentioned, members of his political coalition may have their own different priorities and interests. In January 2025, the Constitutional Court removed the minimum thresholds of 20 percent of parliamentary seats or 25 percent of legislative election votes required to nominate a presidential candidate, abolishing the presidential threshold for now.

Nonetheless, Prabowo’s coalition parties are currently proposing additional requirements for the presidential threshold ruling to limit the number of presidential nominees. This forms part of the deliberation of the amendment to the Election Law that is currently being reviewed by the Indonesian parliament. Nonetheless, smaller political parties within Prabowo’s coalition certainly perceive the threshold as a significant stumbling block for their survival. Reports of fractures within Prabowo’s coalition due to the convergent interests in revising election laws have recently surfaced.

Managing the potential internal friction within Gerindra is another task awaiting Prabowo. In August 2025, the president appointed Sugiono, and until recently Indonesia’s foreign minister, one of his closest confidants, as the party’s secretary general, replacing senior party figure Ahmad Muzani. The appointment is significant because the secretary general’s role extends well beyond running the party’s day-to-day affairs. Under Indonesia’s election law, presidential and legislative nominations must be endorsed by both the party’s chairman (ketua umum) and its secretary general. This gives the secretary general position considerable authority over who stands for office. Thus, Sugiono is likely to play a central role in managing and consolidating Gerindra’s internal dynamics in the lead-up to 2029.

Prabowo’s failure to handle the challenges of maintaining coalition cohesion and managing internal party dynamics will consequently jeopardize the seemingly stable situation amongst the political elites. While the 2029 elections might still be far off, the maneuvers and the stakes of the electoral competition are already becoming apparent.
